Marcel Breuer, club chair B 3 (“Wassily”)

The first tubular steel armchair for the home: a cubic frame of bent tubes with fabric straps for seat, back, and arms.

Source
Bauhaus Kooperation: Clubsessel B 3, 2. Version
Creator
Marcel Breuer
Made
1926 (second version, per Bauhaus Kooperation); first version 1925
Style
Bauhaus (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Constructive, technical, open
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected, in the scratchpad only, the Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau photograph on the Bauhaus Kooperation page and a side view by Sailko of the example in the Musée national d’art moderne, Paris.
Reviewed
25 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Bauhaus Kooperation says Breuer, the junior master in charge of the Dessau furniture workshop, designed the chair in 1926 as a showpiece of new living; it was later called “Wassily” after Wassily Kandinsky, and it furnished the Dessau Bauhaus building. Bauhaus Kooperation.

The Commons photograph labels the Paris example “B 3, 1925.” Commons. MoMA dates its example 1927–1928. MoMA 2851.

Observed

  • The frame is made of thin metal tubes with a worn, dull plating, bent into rectangles with rounded corners.
  • Seen from the side, the base, arms, and back form overlapping rectangles and one strong diagonal.
  • Dark fabric straps stretch between the tubes to form the seat, the back, and the arm rests.
  • Screws and joins in the frame are visible.
  • The chair is open: the floor and the wall show through it from every side.

Why it belongs

The chair turns the poster grammar of bars and one diagonal into a structure. Tubular steel and canvas are shown as they are.

Borrow

Draw with thin continuous lines and rounded corners only where a material bends.

Let one diagonal cross an otherwise orthogonal frame.

A growing catalogue of visual references. Rights and removal
